tagline: A winding forest road climbs to a ridge above the Rio Grande
intro: NM 536 winds up the eastern side of the Sandia Mountains to a dead end at Sandia Crest. The climb reaches a ridge forested mainly with spruce and fir. The Forest Service calls the route the Sandia Crest National Scenic Byway and highlights its panoramic views of Central New Mexico and sheltered picnic grounds.

The Forest Service completed a dirt road to the crest in 1927. Paving followed in 1960 to improve access to La Madera Ski Area. The new road replaced a journey through potholes and mud; sections of the old dirt road remain visible south of it. La Madera became Sandia Peak Ski Area in 1962. Another proposal, Skyline Drive, would have extended a road along the crest. By autumn 1969, five miles of forest had been cleared, but a campaign of postcards and petitions halted construction.

Start at NM 14 in San Antonito and follow NM 536 toward the ski area’s base on the east slope. Continue to Sandia Crest, where a viewing area and communications towers occupy the road’s end. The west side drops toward Albuquerque and the Rio Grande Valley, while the eastern slope descends toward the plains.

moments.title: Sandia Peak Ski Area
moments.text: La Madera began with a rope tow, not a chairlift. The Albuquerque Ski Club cleared runs at Tree Springs in 1935 and opened the ski area the following year. Its 1,500-foot tow offered two rides for 50 cents. A second tow followed in 1937, along with a lodge built with Civilian Conservation Corps help. The resort closed to the public during World War II. Afterward, a T-bar lift replaced the upper rope tow in 1946. Road access comes from the east via NM 536; the tramway approaches from the Albuquerque side and delivers riders to the ski summit.

moments.title: Kiwanis Cabin
moments.text: Kiwanis Cabin is a stone ruin on the crest between Sandia Crest House and the ski resort. Its pueblo-style architecture overlooks the Rio Grande Valley. Hikers visit the ruins; the cabin is an excursion along the ridge.

moments.title: Sandia Crest
moments.text: Sandia Crest is a long ridge rather than a pointed summit. Its western side drops more than 4,000 feet in two horizontal miles toward the Rio Grande Valley and Albuquerque. Spruce and fir cover much of the crest, where radio and television antennas also stand. The road ends at a viewing area by Sandia Crest House. The tramway reaches a different point on the crestline, about 1.5 miles south of Sandia Crest, above the ski area. The crest also marks the western boundary of an 1819 land grant established by Governor Facundo Melgares, which included San Miguel de Carnuel and San Antonio Pueblo.

practical: Sandia Crest: Parking at designated developed recreation sites requires an amenity fee or pass. (checked 2026-10-11)
